screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn the core skills needed to configure and verify network connectivity on a RHEL server. screens.title: NetworkManager — what it is and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkManager is the background service responsible for detecting network hardware, applying connection profiles, and keeping links active. It maintains a set of named connection profiles that include addressing, DNS, and device bindings. This is important because rather than editing a handful of separate files manually, you can create consistent profiles that persist and can be brought up or down predictably. For example, a server may have a profile named my-static-eth0 that assigns a static IP and DNS so monitoring tools can reach it reliably. A common misconception is that NetworkManager is only for desktops; in modern RHEL it is the standard network control point for servers as well. When a network behaves unexpectedly, check whether NetworkManager replaced a manual configuration or applied an unintended DHCP lease. In practice, knowing where NetworkManager stores profiles and how it activates them lets you automate deployments and recover from misconfiguration faster. To test your understanding, ask: when a link comes up with the wrong DNS, do you check the profile or the DHCP lease first? NetworkManager — what it is and why it matters means a system daemon that stores and applies connection profiles so network state is consistent and manageable.. In practical terms, the daemon that controls network state on rhel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › NetworkManager — what it is and why it matters
Definition
NetworkManager is a dynamic configuration daemon that manages devices, connections, and name resolution settings.
Why it matters
  • It centralizes profiles so servers stay reachable with predictable addresses.
  • It supports both DHCP and manual methods for flexibility across environments.
  • Knowing its state helps you diagnose whether a profile or an external DHCP server set values.
Common misconception
Some think NetworkManager is only for desktops; in RHEL it is the primary networking control service even for servers.
Concrete example
A server profile named my-static-eth0 assigns a static address, gateway, and DNS so monitoring and backups can always reach the host at the same IP.
Key takeaway
Treat NetworkManager as the first place to check and configure network state on modern RHEL systems.
Check your understanding
If a server receives the wrong DNS after boot, should you inspect the connection profile or resolv.conf first? Answer: check the active profile and NetworkManager settings, then resolv.conf if needed.

screens.title: nmcli — the command-line toolkit
screens.narratorSegment: nmcli is a scriptable interface to NetworkManager that is ideal for automation and precise server configuration. You can list active connections, inspect profiles, create new connections, and bring them up or down. For example, listing active connections verifies what profile is currently bound to an interface. When creating a new static profile you supply type, connection name, interface name, address, gateway, and DNS. After creating the profile, you must explicitly set the ipv4. method to manual for persistence, then bring the connection up. A common misconception is that supplying an IP alone makes the change permanent; without setting the method to manual it may still use DHCP. In practice, use nmcli in deployment scripts to ensure reproducible network state. Practice by deleting a default system connection, adding a named static profile, modifying its method, and activating it. As you work, confirm with ip addr show and ping to validate addressing and reachability. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › nmcli — the command-line toolkit
Common nmcli workflow
  1. List active connections to identify current profiles.
  2. Create a new connection profile with addressing and DNS fields.
  3. Set ipv4.method to manual for static setups.
  4. Bring the connection up and verify with ip and ping.
Example commands
# List active connections
nmcli connection show --active

# Add a static ethernet profile (example values)
nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name static-eth0 ifname enp0s3 ip4 192.168.1.100/24 gw4 192.168.1.1 dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"

# Ensure it's manual and bring it up
nmcli connection modify static-eth0 ipv4.method manual
nmcli connection up static-eth0
Explanation points
  • connection add creates a named profile stored by NetworkManager for persistence.
  • modify with ipv4.method manual is necessary to make the address assignment persistent.
  • connection up activates the profile immediately so you can verify reachability.
Check after change
Use ip addr show and ping a known IP and a hostname to confirm both routing and DNS.
Common mistake
Forgetting to set ipv4.method to manual, which can cause a static address to be ignored or overridden.

screens.title: Hands-on nmcli: configure a static IP
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete nmcli sequence to configure a static IP and verify it. First, identify your interface with ip addr show so you know the device name like enp0s3. Next, remove an undesired default connection if it exists so names do not conflict. Then add a new connection with type ethernet, a clear connection name, the ifname, the ip4 address and prefix, the gateway, and DNS servers. After adding, explicitly set ipv4. method to manual to ensure the configuration is persistent. Bring the connection up and then run ip addr show for that interface to confirm the assigned address. Finally, ping a known IP to confirm routing, and ping a hostname to confirm DNS. A usual trap is missing double quotes around multiple DNS entries or forgetting to activate the new profile after creation. When automating, script these commands in the order shown and include checks for active connection state. Ask yourself: if ping to an IP works but a hostname fails, where do you look next? Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on nmcli: configure a static IP
Starter checklist
  • Identify interface with ip addr show.
  • Remove or disable conflicting default connection names.
  • Add a named static profile and set method to manual.
  • Bring the profile up and verify with ping and ip commands.
Lab commands (visual only)
# Identify interface
ip addr show

# (Optional) Delete a default connection
sudo nmcli connection delete "System enp0s3"

# Add static profile - example values
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name my-static-eth0 ifname enp0s3 ip4 192.168.1.100/24 gw4 192.168.1.1 dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0

# Verify
ip addr show enp0s3
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
ping -c 3 google.com
Explanation and traps
  • Deleting a default connection avoids naming collisions when adding a new profile with the same interface.
  • Setting ipv4.method to manual is essential; otherwise NetworkManager may keep using DHCP.
  • Confirm both IP-level reachability and DNS resolution; they test different parts of the network stack.
Concrete scenario
You set a static IP for a backup server so nightly backups always target the same address. Verify connections on completion.

screens.title: IP Addressing, Netmask, Gateway, and DNS
screens.narratorSegment: An IP address identifies your device on a network. The netmask divides that address into network and host portions, telling your system which addresses are local and which require a gateway. The gateway is the router your host sends traffic to when the destination is outside the local subnet. DNS servers translate human names into IP addresses, so a working network without correct DNS can still reach raw IPs but fail to resolve domain names. When you assign a static IP, you must supply the netmask or prefix length, the gateway IP, and at least one DNS server, otherwise clients and services that rely on names will fail. A typical mistake is entering an incorrect gateway, which makes external networks unreachable even though the local link appears up. Always confirm the routing table with ip route show after assigning a gateway. As a quick mental checklist: IP tells who you are, netmask tells who is local, gateway tells where to send non-local traffic, and DNS translates names to numbers. IP Addressing, Netmask, Gateway, and DNS means ip = identity, netmask = local scope, gateway = default path off-network, dns = name resolution service.. In practical terms, what each piece does and why it matters for reachability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › IP Addressing, Netmask, Gateway, and DNS
Core definitions
IP address: the numerical identity of a network interface.
Netmask: defines subnet boundaries and host capacity.
Gateway: router used for traffic outside the local subnet.
DNS: service that resolves domain names to IP addresses.
Misconfiguration traps
  • Wrong gateway leaves external networks unreachable despite local link up.
  • Incorrect DNS yields successful pings to IPs but failed hostname resolution.
Concrete example
Assign 192.168.1.100/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 8.8.8.8 so the server can reach both local hosts and internet hosts by name.
Key takeaway
Always provide address, netmask, gateway, and DNS when configuring a static IP to ensure full connectivity.
Check your understanding
If you can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot ping google.com, which subsystem is likely misconfigured? Answer: DNS.

screens.title: Verify network connectivity and troubleshoot
screens.narratorSegment: Verification and troubleshooting follow a predictable order that helps you isolate the layer at fault. Start by checking interface state and addresses with ip addr show. Next, inspect the routing table with ip route show to confirm your default gateway is present. If routing looks correct, test raw connectivity with ping to a public IP; success here tells you packets leave and return. If ping to an IP works but hostnames fail, check DNS by viewing /etc/resolv. conf to see which servers were configured. When packets appear to drop at an intermediate hop, use traceroute or tracepath to identify where traffic stops. A common trap is assuming services are down when the firewall is blocking them; always verify that firewalld allows the required service for the zone. Practically, work top-down: link, route, name resolution, then firewall and service. After each check, note what worked and what failed; this will tell you the next focused check and reduce trial-and-error. Verify network connectivity and troubleshoot means check link and addresses, then routing, then raw ip reachability, then dns, and finally firewall and service configuration.. In practical terms, use ip, ip route, ping, traceroute, and resolv.conf for diagnosis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Verify network connectivity and troubleshoot
Step-by-step checks
  1. ip addr show — confirm the interface is up and has the expected address.
  2. ip route show — ensure a default route points to the configured gateway.
  3. ping a public IP — tests raw reachability through routing and gateway.
  4. ping a hostname — tests DNS resolution; if it fails, inspect /etc/resolv.conf.
  5. traceroute or tracepath — identify where a path fails between hosts.
Commands (visual)
ip addr show
ip route show
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
ping -c 3 google.com
traceroute google.com
cat /etc/resolv.conf
Illustrative example
If ping to 8.8.8.8 succeeds but ping to google.com fails, resolv.conf likely points to incorrect DNS servers. If both pings fail, check ip route show for missing default gateway.
Common mistake
Jumping to restart services before checking addressing and DNS often wastes time; always verify network layers first.
Key takeaway
Work top-down: link, route, reachability, name resolution, firewall, then service.

screens.title: Resolving DNS issues and resolv.conf
screens.narratorSegment: DNS resolution depends on correct server entries and on how NetworkManager or local resolvers populate /etc/resolv. conf. If you can reach an IP but not a hostname, the issue is almost always name resolution rather than routing. Inspect /etc/resolv. conf to see which name servers the system will query. NetworkManager can manage resolv. conf directly or hand off to a local caching resolver depending on configuration. When configuring static addresses, ensure DNS entries are included in the profile so resolv. conf contains the intended servers. A common mistake is editing resolv. conf manually when NetworkManager overwrites it; instead modify the connection profile or the NetworkManager configuration so changes persist. In troubleshooting, use dig or nslookup if available to test queries against a specific DNS server. The practical rule is: confirm IP reachability first, then test names and verify resolv. conf and the connection profile if names fail. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Resolving DNS issues and resolv.conf
Why names fail
  • resolv.conf points to wrong or unreachable DNS servers.
  • NetworkManager overwrote manual edits on shutdown or restart.
  • Local caching resolvers alter query behavior if misconfigured.
Practical checks
  • Ping a known IP to confirm routing.
  • Inspect /etc/resolv.conf for configured servers.
  • Use dig or nslookup against a server to test queries directly.
Example scenario
You can ping 8.8.8.8 but not google.com. /etc/resolv.conf lists only internal servers that are offline. The fix is to update the connection's DNS entries and reactivate the profile so NetworkManager writes the correct resolv.conf.
Common mistake
Manually editing resolv.conf without updating the connection profile leads to changes being overwritten by NetworkManager.
Key takeaway
Update DNS through NetworkManager profiles so entries persist and resolv.conf reflects intended servers.

screens.title: firewalld — zones and services
screens.narratorSegment: firewalld provides a dynamic firewall abstraction based on zones, which represent different trust levels for network connections or interfaces. Zones like public, internal, and dmz map to sets of allowed services and ports. By default firewalld blocks most incoming connections; you explicitly add services to the appropriate zone to allow traffic. For example, adding the ssh service to the public zone allows remote administrative access. Zones let you expose services selectively depending on the network the interface is connected to. A common misconception is that opening a port once is sufficient; in firewalld you must decide whether the change should be temporary or permanent. If you forget the --permanent flag, changes will be lost on reload. After making permanent changes remember to reload firewalld so they take effect. Always verify zone membership and the list of allowed services when securing a server. firewalld — zones and services means use zones to express trust levels and add only needed services; prefer permanent changes for lasting configuration and reload to apply them.. In practical terms, control trust and exposure with zones and named services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › firewalld — zones and services
Zones explained
  • public: for untrusted networks; only explicitly allowed services are accessible.
  • internal: for trusted networks where more services may be allowed.
  • dmz: for servers exposed to the internet but isolated from internal networks.
Service management
To allow a service in a zone, use firewall-cmd with --add-service and consider --permanent followed by --reload to apply persistent changes.
Concrete example
To allow HTTP permanently in the public zone: add the http service with --permanent and then reload firewalld to apply changes.
Common mistake
Forgetting --permanent or forgetting to reload after a permanent change are the most common sources of confusion.
Key takeaway
Always decide if a change should be temporary or permanent and confirm with firewall-cmd --list-services for the zone.

screens.title: firewall-cmd examples and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: firewall-cmd is the command-line interface for firewalld that lets you add or remove services and ports by zone. A typical workflow is to add a service to the public zone permanently, then reload firewalld so the change is applied. For example, allowing SSH or HTTP ensures remote administration and web access as required. Use firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public to confirm what is open. A frequent mistake is to leave changes temporary during testing, forgetting to make them permanent, and being surprised after a reboot. Another trap is not checking the zone associated with an interface; adding a service to the wrong zone has no effect for that interface. When automating firewall changes, include both the --permanent flag and a reload step. Finally, always verify from a separate client machine that the service is reachable and the intended ports are open. Which check would you run first if a newly added service is still unreachable from a client? firewall-cmd examples and common pitfalls means add services with --permanent for lasting changes, reload to apply, and verify the zone and list of services to confirm access.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › firewall-cmd examples and common pitfalls
Common commands
# Allow HTTP permanently in public zone, then reload
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public

# Allow SSH permanently
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public
Verify from a different host that the service port is reachable after changes.
Explanation and traps
  • --permanent stores the change so it persists across reloads and reboots.
  • --reload applies all permanent changes to the runtime configuration.
  • Confirm the interface is in the intended zone; otherwise the rule will not affect it.
Common mistake
Not using --permanent for intended lasting changes, or forgetting to reload, leads to temporary-only changes.
Check your understanding
If a port remains closed after a permanent add and reload, verify the zone of the interface and that the service name maps to the expected port.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on activity: configure static IP and enable SSH
Lab steps
  1. Identify interface: ip addr show.
  2. Create a static profile with nmcli and set ipv4.method to manual.
  3. Activate the profile and verify with ip addr show and ping.
  4. Allow SSH permanently with firewall-cmd and reload.
  5. From a client, SSH to the new static IP to confirm access.
Commands (lab reference)
# Example sequence
ip addr show
sudo nmcli connection delete "System enp0s3"
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name my-static-eth0 ifname enp0s3 ip4 192.168.1.100/24 gw4 192.168.1.1 dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli connection modify my-static-eth0 ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli connection up my-static-eth0

# Firewall
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public

# From client
ssh user@192.168.1.100
Lab tip
Run verification steps between changes so you can isolate which action produced the expected result.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn the core skills needed to configure and verify network connectivity on a RHEL server. We will treat NetworkManager as the central service you will interact with, and show both the scriptable command-line tool nmcli and the user-friendly text interface nmtui. You will learn what an IP address, netmask, gateway, and DNS server actually do, and how to check your settings with commands like ip, ping, and traceroute. Finally, we will cover basic firewall management with firewalld and how zones control exposure of services like SSH and HTTP. These skills matter because servers must have stable addressing, reliable name resolution, and minimal exposed services to be secure and reachable. For example, a web server needs a fixed IP and an open HTTP port in the firewall to be reachable from clients. A common misconception is that a service restart fixes all connectivity problems; often the issue is DNS or firewall rules, not the service itself. Keep that question in mind as we proceed: when a server cannot be reached, what layers do you check first?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to configure interfaces using nmcli and nmtui, manage NetworkManager, verify connectivity, and implement basic firewall rules. First, configuring interfaces lets you assign static addresses so services stay reachable. For example, a database server needs a predictable IP so clients can always connect. Second, managing NetworkManager is important because it is the system component that applies and persists those settings. Third, verification skills using ip, ping, and traceroute let you confirm both addressing and reachability before blaming services. A common error is assuming a restarted service fixes network problems when the real issue is DNS or a missing route. Finally, learning firewalld means you control which services are accessible; opening only SSH and HTTP reduces attack surface. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you recall the steps, and a verified competency milestone you can self-check against. Keep an eye on the checklist: configure, verify, secure, and when in doubt, check DNS and firewall rules first.

This second objectives slide ties each skill to practical tasks you will perform. For configuring interfaces, you will create a profile for an Ethernet interface and make it persistent so services remain reachable after reboots. For NetworkManager, you will query active profiles and restart the daemon when recovering from a broken configuration. For verification, you will run ip addr show and ip route show, then ping a DNS server and a domain name to separate reachability from name resolution. For the firewall, you will add services to a zone permanently and reload firewalld, then confirm that only intended ports are open. A frequent mistake is forgetting to make a firewall change permanent or forgetting to reload after a permanent change; both leave services inaccessible later. Each card below includes a small mnemonic and the verified competency milestone to guide practice sessions. Work through these steps in a terminal environment to internalize the commands and checks.

NetworkManager is the background service responsible for detecting network hardware, applying connection profiles, and keeping links active. It maintains a set of named connection profiles that include addressing, DNS, and device bindings. This is important because rather than editing a handful of separate files manually, you can create consistent profiles that persist and can be brought up or down predictably. For example, a server may have a profile named my-static-eth0 that assigns a static IP and DNS so monitoring tools can reach it reliably. A common misconception is that NetworkManager is only for desktops; in modern RHEL it is the standard network control point for servers as well. When a network behaves unexpectedly, check whether NetworkManager replaced a manual configuration or applied an unintended DHCP lease. In practice, knowing where NetworkManager stores profiles and how it activates them lets you automate deployments and recover from misconfiguration faster. To test your understanding, ask: when a link comes up with the wrong DNS, do you check the profile or the DHCP lease first? NetworkManager — what it is and why it matters means a system daemon that stores and applies connection profiles so network state is consistent and manageable.. In practical terms, the daemon that controls network state on rhel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

nmcli is a scriptable interface to NetworkManager that is ideal for automation and precise server configuration. You can list active connections, inspect profiles, create new connections, and bring them up or down. For example, listing active connections verifies what profile is currently bound to an interface. When creating a new static profile you supply type, connection name, interface name, address, gateway, and DNS. After creating the profile, you must explicitly set the ipv4. method to manual for persistence, then bring the connection up. A common misconception is that supplying an IP alone makes the change permanent; without setting the method to manual it may still use DHCP. In practice, use nmcli in deployment scripts to ensure reproducible network state. Practice by deleting a default system connection, adding a named static profile, modifying its method, and activating it. As you work, confirm with ip addr show and ping to validate addressing and reachability. What step would you take first when automating a static configuration on a new server? nmcli — the command-line toolkit means use nmcli for repeatable, scriptable network profiles and always set ipv4.method to manual for static addresses.. In practical terms, list, add, modify, and activate connections with nmcli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a concrete nmcli sequence to configure a static IP and verify it. First, identify your interface with ip addr show so you know the device name like enp0s3. Next, remove an undesired default connection if it exists so names do not conflict. Then add a new connection with type ethernet, a clear connection name, the ifname, the ip4 address and prefix, the gateway, and DNS servers. After adding, explicitly set ipv4. method to manual to ensure the configuration is persistent. Bring the connection up and then run ip addr show for that interface to confirm the assigned address. Finally, ping a known IP to confirm routing, and ping a hostname to confirm DNS. A usual trap is missing double quotes around multiple DNS entries or forgetting to activate the new profile after creation. When automating, script these commands in the order shown and include checks for active connection state. Ask yourself: if ping to an IP works but a hostname fails, where do you look next? Hands-on nmcli: configure a static IP means identify the interface, add a named profile with ip, set ipv4.method to manual, bring it up, and verify reachability and name resolution.. In practical terms, step-by-step example you can run in a rhel terminal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

nmtui provides a guided, menu-driven interface for NetworkManager that is useful on systems without a graphical desktop. It presents options to edit connections, activate or deactivate them, and set hostnames in an accessible curses layout. This is helpful when you prefer interactive fields over typing many command arguments, for example when setting a static IP manually on a single host. Use nmtui to choose the interface, fill IP, netmask, gateway, and DNS, then save and activate. A common misconception is that nmtui cannot be used on servers; it is specifically designed for terminal-only environments. However, while convenient for manual edits, nmtui is not scriptable, so for automation use nmcli. An IP address identifies your device on a network. The netmask divides that address into network and host portions, telling your system which addresses are local and which require a gateway. The gateway is the router your host sends traffic to when the destination is outside the local subnet. DNS servers translate human names into IP addresses, so a working network without correct DNS can still reach raw IPs but fail to resolve domain names. When you assign a static IP, you must supply the netmask or prefix length, the gateway IP, and at least one DNS server, otherwise clients and services that rely on names will fail. A typical mistake is entering an incorrect gateway, which makes external networks unreachable even though the local link appears up. Always confirm the routing table with ip route show after assigning a gateway. DNS resolution depends on correct server entries and on how NetworkManager or local resolvers populate /etc/resolv. conf. firewalld provides a dynamic firewall abstraction based on zones, which represent different trust levels for network connections or interfaces. Zones like public, internal, and dmz map to sets of allowed services and ports. By default firewalld blocks most incoming connections; you explicitly add services to the appropriate zone to allow traffic. For example, adding the ssh service to the public zone allows remote administrative access. Zones let you expose services selectively depending on the network the interface is connected to. A common misconception is that opening a port once is sufficient; in firewalld you must decide whether the change should be temporary or permanent. If you forget the --permanent flag, changes will be lost on reload. After making permanent changes remember to reload firewalld so they take effect.
